# Construct the Minimum Bitwise Array I. -1 marks a prime with no answer.

@example 17 | 18 = 10001 | 10010 = 10011 = 19 and 40 | 41 = 41; a | (a + 1) is always odd, so nothing gives 2.
[19,2,41]
=> [17,-1,40]

@example 127 is 1111111 in binary: 63 | 64 = 127. For 23 (10111), 19 | 20 = 10011 | 10100 = 10111.
[127,23]
=> [63,19]

@example 39, 43, 45 and 46 all give 47 (101111); the smallest is 39.
[47]
=> [39]

# The smallest prime, the only even one, has no answer.
[2]
=> [-1]

# The smallest odd prime: 1 | 2 = 3.
[3]
=> [1]

# 2s mixed with repeated primes.
[2,5,2,5]
=> [-1,4,-1,4]

[2,2,2]
=> [-1,-1,-1]

# Primes ending in 01 in binary: the answer is p - 1, the largest a worth
# trying. 997 is the largest prime allowed.
[17,89,101,997]
=> [16,88,100,996]

# Primes ending in 011: p - 1 works too, but p - 2 is smaller.
[43,59,83]
=> [41,57,81]

# Mersenne primes, all 1s in binary: the run of trailing 1s is the whole
# number.
[7,31,127]
=> [3,15,63]

# Runs of 3 to 7 trailing 1s with a 0 above them: 151 is 10010111, 79 is
# 1001111, 991 is 1111011111, 191 is 10111111 and 383 is 101111111.
[151,79,991,191,383]
=> [147,71,975,159,319]

# The answers keep the order of nums.
[997,2,3,991]
=> [996,-1,1,975]

# Random small cases from gen.c (lc check --regen makes them).
@gen 1 small
[5,41,97]
=> [4,40,96]

@gen 2 small
[223,3,59,31,83]
=> [207,1,57,15,81]

@gen 3 small
[2,19,2,2,79,7]
=> [-1,17,-1,-1,71,3]

@gen 4 small
[97,383]
=> [96,319]

@gen 5 small
[79,47,71,17]
=> [71,39,67,16]

@gen 6 small
[7,37,41,31]
=> [3,36,40,15]
